name: Dakota
catalog_quote: (d) Dakota (Siouan, Great Plains; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1985a, 1985b). Stress falls on the second syllable of a word, and on monosyllables. This suggests that a single even iamb is assigned at the left edge of a word.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (strict OUT with out_code 'lexical', dominant IN, rule 01 010 0100... kept as the dominant peninitial rule) — unless the catalog owner rules that the Siouan DAR's initial-stress class counts as derived (epenthetic-a CVC stems, contractions) rather than lexical; whichever way it is ruled, apply the same ruling to the sibling records lako1247 (Boas & Deloria 1941: 'not firmly attached to any particular syllable') and assi1247, which are coded fixed-strict on the same rule.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the verified primary quotation (Riggs 1893:5 §4.2) and the database quotation (Hayes 1995:267 + fn.19) are present verbatim in held files at the stated places. (2) Source quality: the peninitial rule is multiply and consistently attested — Riggs 1893 (Santee, primary), Boas & Deloria 1941 §23 (Teton), Shaw 1985a:175 via StressTyp2, Hayes 1995:267, Kennedy 1994:47 — so the rule string 01/010/0100... is secure and dialect-appropriate. But the modern primary analyses (Shaw 1980, Shaw 1985a, Chambers 1978) and the 2024 Santee-Sisseton grammar are not held; the record rests on an 1893 missionary grammar plus a 1995 survey paragraph. (3) The risk is the STRICT register, whose catalog definition is 'one determinate weight-blind pattern per word length, exceptions falsify'. sources.citation: Kennedy, Christopher. 1994. Morphological alignment and head projection [Exceptional stress in Dakota]. Phonology at Santa Cruz 3: 47-64.
sources.quote: p.47: 'Most surface forms in Dakota are characterized by stress on the second syllable from the left edge of the word' (data from Shaw 1976, 1985: čhikté, wičháyakte, owį́čhayaktepiktešni); 'both Shaw (1985) and Sietsema (1988) claim that syllable weight plays no role in determining stress in Dakota'. p.48: 'not all occurrences of stress in Dakota obey this constraint ... three sets of surface forms in which stress falls on the initial syllable': bisyllabic CVC-root nouns with epenthetic final a (čhápa, šúŋka, čéka), plus compound/clitic cases.
sources.locator: p.47 §1.1 'Regular stress'; pp.48-49 §1.2 'Irregular stress' (1.2.1 CVC roots)

sources.citation: Patterson, Trudi Alice. 1990. Theoretical aspects of Dakota morphology and phonology. PhD dissertation, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (IDEALS item 22681, hdl 2142/22546) — item page only; PDF is Illinois-restricted.
sources.quote: Abstract states the thesis 'investigates some morphological and phonological processes in Lakota' within Lexical Phonology (syllable structure, reduplication, infixation); despite the title it is a Lakota (lako1247) study and the full text is restricted, so no stress statement could be read.
